rationale: A wins because it keeps the strongest story cleanly framed around ownership and then forces the missing-proof problem into the open. "On will rent you a running shoe you can never own" is sharper and more editor-ready than B's softer "On takes its shoe subscription nationwide, betting runners will rent rather than own." B is good, but its "funding-mechanics" angle mislabels a public-company business-model story and pads into investor speculation faster than the facts can carry it.
gaps_in_A: "The castor bean is quietly becoming a running-shoe raw material" is plausible but soft; without volume, supplier, or sourcing data, it is a demand-signal question more than a ready trend story.
"runners track shoe mileage obsessively" is a fair beat insight, but it is not in the update; A should flag it as a reporter-context assumption rather than a fact it can lean on.

The contrarian angle is strong, but "a national program with undisclosed numbers is a story" slightly overstates it; without return-rate refusal or an external claim-standard hook, it is still a sharp question first.
gaps_in_B: "Story type: funding-mechanics" is the wrong label; there is no funding event, and the supplied facts support a markets/business-model angle, not financing mechanics.
"shareholders should care or ignore it" drifts past the update. There are no subscriber counts, price, revenue materiality, analyst comments, or market reaction in the facts.
"The other kept angles drop to the material, the balance sheet, and the runner" oversells the balance-sheet angle; per-unit economics are undisclosed, so the balance sheet is mostly absent.

"Nationwide means which country?" is useful diligence, but the update says Company: On and nationwide subscription; treating the country as unknown is a bit too cute unless the source copy itself omitted geography.
